Our customers and partners talk to us in about sixty Slack channels, and Conclude carries the Teams ones. This report compares the tools that broadcast into those channels and recommends a skill we build ourselves. It needs no new seats.

01 · What we found
01 — What we found

Every customer channel already runs through our own Slack.

Each customer gets a channel in our workspace, named <customer>-lleverage. Customers on Slack join it through Slack Connect. Conclude links the channels of customers on Teams to their own Teams channel. Sitech is one example: Conclude connected #sitech-lleverage to Sitech-Lleverage / General on 25 September. A message posted on our side reaches both platforms, so we only have to post in Slack.

Tools today that post to many at once

What gets in the way

  • Slack posts to one channel at a time. Workflow Builder needs one step per channel, drops rich formatting and breaks when the list changes.
  • Conclude cannot broadcast. It syncs channel pairs, one to one. It has no announcement feature and no public API for one. It bills per internal user ($12–16 a month) and charges $5 a month for each external channel beyond the 10 in Pro.
  • The channel list is messy. The ~60 channels mix live customers, partners (Incentro, Twofeetup), vendors (WorkOS), pilots and dormant accounts. Whatever we choose, someone has to curate the list of who receives which update.
  • Language differs. Most of the base is Dutch. An update in English only reaches some readers less well.

02 · Options
02 — Options compared

The tools that broadcast to Teams cost $3,000 to $12,000 a year.

Pylon, Plain and ClearFeed are support desks with a broadcast feature added on. With them we would pay for a ticket queue we do not need. Changelog tools publish a page and send email, but they do not post into a customer's channel. List prices are from the vendors' sites in October 2026.

03 · Recommended setup
03 — Recommended setup

A broadcast skill: draft from #change-log, approve, post to the list.

It follows the feature-drop pattern we already run. A Claude skill writes the update from #change-log and the PR descriptions. You approve it on a Linear issue. A small script then posts it through a Slack app that has only the chat:write permission. Nothing goes out until you approve.

Source#change-log posts and PRs from the week
DraftSkill writes EN and NL in our voice; flagged items marked
ApproveBadr picks the audience and says yes on Linear
PostScript posts to every channel on the list, ~1 a second
LogMessage links saved; replies read back from the threads

The channel list

One file in the autopilot repo. Each channel has an audience (customer, partner, pilot), a language (EN or NL), its platform (Slack, or Teams via Conclude) and the feature flags the customer has. Badr curates it once. After that, new *-lleverage channels show up as "to classify".

Surveys, phase two

Interactive Slack buttons are unlikely to survive the Conclude bridge, so a survey is a link to a short form, such as Tally on its free plan. The script tags each link with the channel, so answers come back per customer. Native buttons can come later for customers on Slack only.

Format rules that keep it working on Teams

  • Plain Slack markdown: a bold title, three to five bullets and one link. Block Kit layouts and buttons are unlikely to render after the bridge. Step 01 tests this too.
  • One message per channel and no @channel. Customers who want more detail can ask in the thread, where the account owner sees it.
  • The bot has to be invited to every channel on the list, private ones included. The script shows the channels it cannot reach yet.

Option: run it as a Lleverage workflow

The same flow can run on our own platform: a data table holds the channel list, a schedule runs it, an approval step waits for you and a Slack node posts. It takes more effort to build. In return, the team can see it and trigger it without Claude Code, and we can show it as our own operations running on Lleverage.

What happens next

One test in a bridged channel decides the route.

Step 01 · 1 day

Test the bridge

Create the Slack app and post one bot message in a test channel bridged to Teams. Check that it arrives as readable text.

Step 02 · 1 hour

Curate the list

Autopilot drafts the list of ~60 channels with a best guess for each. Badr corrects the audience, language and flags.

Step 03 · 2–3 days

Build the skill

Draft, approve, post and log. First run: last week's feature drop, sent to five friendly customers.
